svg.text: GP-W1 Gritty produce: dunk basket over a sediment trap
Sand sinks, leaves float with the water: plunge, let it settle, lift the leaves out — repeat until the drain water is clear.
G-produce · wash leek, spinach, lamb’s lettuce (H)
basket holes Ø 5 · quiet zone 40 mm
3 L per bath · plunge 20 × 1–1.5 Hz, 50 mm
stop when the turbidity sensor reads clear
SECTION — dunk basket over a sediment trap
40 mm quiet zone: sand settles
here and stays
water line, 3 L cold mains water

g.text: sand falls through the Ø 5 holes
rest 10 s, lift the basket OUT — never pour through the leaves

svg.text: turbidity sensor
2 mm strainer → drain
Why it works
Grit is quartz sand, 0.1–0.5 mm, 2.65 × water density.
In air water films hold it to the leaf; under water
only folds trap it. The plunge flushes the folds
(relative flow 0.15–0.3 m/s).
A 0.3 mm grain falls 40 mm in about 1 s;
leaves are nearly neutral and move with the water.
So: loosen under water, let the sand sink,
lift the leaves out upward.
Usually 2 baths, 3–4 for lamb’s lettuce rosettes.
6–12 L water and 1.5–3 min per 200–300 g.
GP-W4 Leek: cut first, wash afterwards
soil hides between the sheaths
two fence cuts (root, dark green), slice into rings —
the rings open and one bath is usually enough
Washing removes grit, not germs: ≈ 1 log reduction,
the raw-produce safety rules (FSF) still apply.

g.text: 1/6 The basket with the leaves sits in the vessel, 40 mm above the floor; 3 L of cold water fill in.
2/6 The basket plunges 20 times: water flushes the folds, freed sand sinks through the Ø 5 holes.
3/6 Rest 10 s, then the basket is lifted OUT — the sand stays below, the water is never poured through the leaves.
4/6 The water is dumped past a turbidity sensor (a dishwasher part): cloudy → one more bath.
5/6 Bath 2: fresh water, plunge again; the sensor now reads clear.
